facts.text: On this date in 1792, France abolished the monarchy and declared a republic — then proceeded to execute its king, start a war with most of Europe, and invent the guillotine as a symbol of equality.
On this date in 1949, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China to a crowd in Beijing. The country he founded is now the world's largest economy by purchasing power.
Manila is the most densely populated city on Earth — over 111,000 people per square kilometer, roughly 70 times denser than Los Angeles.
More people live inside a circle drawn around Dhaka, Bangladesh than in the entire United States west of the Mississippi River.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, containing roughly 60% of the world's fresh surface water by lake count.
On this date in 1931, Britain abandoned the gold standard. The pound fell 25% in weeks — and the economist who predicted catastrophe if it happened watched the economy promptly improve.
On this date in 2001, the Dow suffered its largest single-day point drop in history at the time: 684 points, the Monday after markets reopened following September 11.
The New York Stock Exchange was founded in 1792 under a buttonwood tree. The 24 brokers who signed the agreement were essentially forming a cartel to fix their own commissions.

Berkshire Hathaway's original business was a failing textile mill. Warren Buffett later called buying it the worst investment of his life — a mistake that cost him roughly $200 billion in compounding.

The entire global derivatives market has a notional value exceeding $600 trillion — roughly six times world GDP. Most of that sum will never actually change hands, but the number never stops shocking people.
On this date in 1956, the first transatlantic telephone cable began service — carrying 36 calls at once. Today a single fiber strand carries over 100 terabits per second.
Your skeleton is not static. Every 10 years, you have an almost entirely new one — bone remodeling silently replaces roughly 10% of your skeleton annually.
On this date in 2003, the Galileo spacecraft was deliberately crashed into Jupiter to prevent contaminating its moons. It had traveled 4.6 billion kilometers.
A neutron star is so dense that a sugar-cube-sized chunk would weigh about 100 million tons on Earth — the mass of a small mountain compressed into near-nothing.
The human eye can detect a single photon of light in complete darkness. Your visual system is operating at the literal physical limit of sensitivity.
On this day in 1937, Tolkien published The Hobbit — a book older than nuclear weapons, the microwave oven, and the transistor.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. When Montezuma was crowned in 1502, Oxford had already been running for 400 years.
On this day in 1780, Benedict Arnold handed West Point's plans to the British. He lived another 21 years, dying in London, never tried for treason.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. The pyramid predates her by 2,500 years.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the telephone, and 134 years before the first iPhone.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in 2012, it spread so fast it feels ancient.
Hiraeth (Welsh, n.): a longing for a home you cannot return to — or one that never existed. English has no equivalent, which says something about English.
On this day in 1780, Benedict Arnold's treason was exposed. The word 'traitor' traces to Latin traditor — one who hands over. Arnold handed over West Point's plans to the British.
Tsundoku (Japanese, n.): buying books and letting them pile up unread. From tsunde (to stack) and oku (to leave). A condition older than the word, finally named.
On this day in 1937, Tolkien published The Hobbit. He invented the word 'tween' — the irresponsible years between childhood and adulthood — decades before pop culture claimed it.
On this date in 2021, El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender — the first nation to do so. The IMF spent the next three years pressuring them to reverse it. They didn't.
On this date in 2017, China banned ICOs outright, freezing $400M in fundraises overnight. Bitcoin dropped 10% in hours, then fully recovered within a week.
Ethereum's gas limit is set by miners — not the protocol. Blocks can exceed it by up to 12.5% per block, a safety valve baked into EIP-1559 that most users never notice.
The FBI seized 144,000 BTC from the Silk Road in 2013. They auctioned it in batches; Tim Draper won 30,000 of them for roughly $19M. At 2024 peak prices, that lot was worth $2.1B.
Bitcoin's smallest unit, the satoshi, wasn't named in Satoshi Nakamoto's whitepaper. The community coined the term in a 2010 BitcoinTalk thread — Nakamoto had already gone silent by then.

Today in 1956, the Dartmouth Summer Research Project proposal — which coined 'artificial intelligence' — was submitted exactly two years after John McCarthy first drafted it, already obsolete before the workshop even ended.
Today in 2021, DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 paper published in Nature, predicting protein structures with atomic accuracy. It solved in months what structural biology had spent 50 years on.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average US homes, for a single model.
The transformer architecture, which underlies nearly every major language model today, was introduced in a 2017 paper by eight authors — six of whom had left Google within two years of publishing it.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), now central to aligning large language models, was first applied to language generation in a 2019 OpenAI paper that attracted little attention at the time of release.
